size.note: Shoulder height and tail length follow Wikipedia, which also splits shoulder height as 140–165 cm in males and 130–145 cm in females, and gives a typical head-and-body length of 3.3–3.45 m and a total length including the tail of 2.90–5.05 m. Mass 1,300–3,200 kg follows Animal Diversity Web. Wikipedia instead gives mean adult weights of about 1,480 kg in bulls and 1,365 kg in cows, with exceptionally large males reaching 2,660 kg; those means are not entered as ranges. No Kruger-specific measurements were found.

summary: A huge, barrel-shaped, almost hairless mammal of rivers and dams. The eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on the head, so the animal can lie almost submerged with only those parts showing. The skin is purplish-grey or bluish-black, pinker around the eyes, ears and underside. Kruger holds a year-round population concentrated on the perennial rivers.
description: Adults are among the heaviest land mammals. The body is barrel-shaped, with short legs and a short tail, and the mouth can open very widely, showing long lower canines and incisors used in fighting. The skin is very thick and nearly hairless, purplish-grey or blue-black on the upperparts and brownish-pink on the underside and around the eyes and ears. A red-orange secretion, sometimes called 'blood sweat', acts as a sunscreen and antibiotic. Males and females are hard to tell apart in the field; cows and young bulls in particular look similar. Calves are much smaller and often stay close to the cow, sometimes on her back in deep water.
habits: Hippos spend most of the day in water, in pods that may be large but with little lasting social bonding between adults. Bulls hold territories in the water, not on land. At dusk they leave the water to graze, usually alone, walking a few kilometres and returning by dawn. In Kruger they concentrate on the perennial rivers, including the Sabie, Crocodile, Olifants, Letaba, Luvuvhu and Limpopo, and on dams. Numbers rise and fall with drought and recovery.

diet.summary: A grazer. The wild diet is almost entirely grass, with only minimal aquatic plants. An animal may eat around 40 kg of grass in a night. Occasional reports of carrion-eating are treated as unusual, not as a regular part of the diet.

young: Cows usually have a single calf after a gestation of about eight months. Conceptions and births peak in the wet season. Calves may be born on land or in shallow water, at an average mass of about 50 kg and an average length of about 127 cm. The cow is very protective. Calves can be carried on the mother's back in deep water, and may be left for a time in a nursery group. They no longer need to suckle at about a year. Exact calving months for Kruger were not found.

predators.note: Adults are rarely taken; calves are more vulnerable.
Not a mammal in this guide; listed because large crocodiles may take calves.

habitat: Permanent water deep enough to immerse in, with gently sloping shores and short-grass grazing within a few kilometres. In Kruger, hippos concentrate on the perennial rivers and on dams.

population.notes: Some sources claim a 2023 Kruger population of 5,889 hippopotamus, given as a count rather than a range. One source describes the Kruger trend as up significantly since the late 1990s, with a dip in the 2015/16 drought. The regional Red List trend is stable. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf. Regional Red List status is Least Concern; the IUCN global assessment is Vulnerable.

viewNotes.note: A barrel-shaped body, short legs, and a huge head with the eyes, ears and nostrils on top.
In water, often only the eyes, ears and nostrils show above the surface.
Calves are much smaller than the adults and may stand on rocks or banks while the adults lie in the water.
Pods rest packed together in the water or along the shore, with calves among the adults.

calls.description: The most common call is a 'wheeze honk': a high-pitched squeal followed by a deeper, resonant call that can travel far in air. Animals can recognise one another's calls. When threatened they produce exhalations, and fighting bulls bellow. They also produce clicks underwater.
